title: Virginia Topples Its Jim Crow-Era Lifetime Ban on Voting
author: Alex Burness
content:
Virginia voters have toppled one of the nation’s harshest felony
disenfranchisement schemes, ending a Jim Crow-era policy of exclusion that has
blocked millions of people from voting since 1902.

Voters approved Amendment 3 on Tuesday, which changed the state constitution
to provide that any citizen can vote so long as they’re not actively
incarcerated over a felony conviction. The state constitution previously held
that anyone convicted of any felony would be disenfranchised for life, unless
a governor personally restored those rights on an individual basis.

Virginia had been one of just three states, along with Iowa and Kentucky,
where the state constitution called for lifetime disenfranchisement for any
felony conviction. Voters erased this rule on Tuesday, approving Amendment 3.
The amendment led 55 to 45 percent with the majority of votes counted just
before 10 p.m. on election night, when the Associated Press called its
victory.

The exclusion reversed by Amendment 3 had been codified in Virginia [124 years
ago](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-governor-youngkin-rights-restoration/) by
explicitly white supremacist state leaders who, after the Civil War,
specifically sought to limit Black political power by harshly policing Black
residents and then tying criminal convictions to voting rights. Their plan
worked as intended: Black voters have been disproportionately blocked from
voting in Virginia for more than a century; [in the 2016
election](https://www.sentencingproject.org/app/uploads/2022/08/6-Million-
Lost-Voters.pdf), for instance, 22 percent of Black adults in Virginia were
disenfranchised, compared to just 4 percent of the rest of the population.

“It's a turning point in the state of Virginia,” George Hawkins, a formerly
disenfranchised man, said of Amendment 3. “It's a turning point for criminal
justice reform. It's powerful, and that's why certain people fought to keep it
this way for so long.”

Hawkins, who is 34, voted for the first time this election. He’d been
convicted as a teenager, and, for years after his 2023 release from prison,
was one of the many [thousands of Virginians blocked from
voting](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-governor-rights-restoration-blocked-
from-voting/) because he had not been personally restored by the governor.

He regained eligibility recently, [thanks to a landmark court ruling earlier
this year](https://boltsmag.org/readmission-acts-and-felony-
disenfranchisement/). In January, a federal judge ruled that Virginia’s
disenfranchisement scheme was unconstitutional because it exceeded guardrails
that Congress had established for former Confederate states during
Reconstruction.

Like lots of other formerly incarcerated Virginians interviewed by _Bolts_ in
recent years, Hawkins characterized his previous disenfranchisement as a loss
not only of voting rights, but of a sense that he and his voice mattered.

“There's a certain pride and a certain belonging that’s associated with
voting,” he said, “and when you take that away from a person, it's very hard
for them to get into the mindset of, ‘I belong.’”

The passage of Amendment 3 ensures in the state constitution that anyone
exiting incarceration will be automatically eligible to register to vote, even
if they’re still finishing out a term of parole or probation.

“When you come home from prison,” Hawkins said, “all you want to do is just
get back to normal. You want to be a part of things, and you are a part of
things: You went to that elementary school, you grew up down the street from
that bakery, you went to that skating rink. But when society tells you your
voice doesn't matter to the things that govern you in your neighborhood, that
type of psychology leads to a person not feeling a part of their community.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/886725518_1693775115449548_3496637548821498578_n-1.jpg)Virginia
Governor Abigail Spanberger campaigns for Amendment 3 with local leaders in
the city of Newport News. (Facebook/Abigail Spanberger)

Voting rights advocates have long been frustrated with the fact that their
state has conferred so much power on the governor to determine whether people
like Hawkins should ever get to vote again. Amendment 3 removes that massive
gubernatorial authority, ensuring that the bounds of felony disenfranchisement
in this state will not change based on the outcome of future gubernatorial
elections.

The last few years have reminded these advocates of why the previous status
quo was so untenable. Though Virginia governors had, since 2013, taken steps
to restore voting rights to hundreds of thousands of people with past
convictions, Republican Glenn Youngkin brought that program to a screeching
halt after he was elected in 2021. Youngkin [dramatically limited voting
rights restorations](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-governor-youngkin-rights-
restoration/), leaving thousands of Virginians, including Hawkins, to wonder
if they’d ever be able to vote again.

Current Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, [reversed Youngkin’s
program](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-governor-restores-voting-rights/) after
taking office earlier this year, and restored voting rights to some 66,000
people in July. Voting rights advocates celebrated that move, but said at the
time that they remained focused on eliminating gubernatorial discretion over
this issue once and for all.

“For one person to be able to have so much control over people like myself is
not right,” said Anthony Martinez, who was released from prison in March and
restored as a voter by Spanberger in July. At 47, he voted this fall for the
first time in his life.

Martinez added, of Amendment 3’s passage, “We can immediately play a part in
what's going on in our community, and not have to hope and pray that you'll be
able to get to the ballot.”

Amendment 3 was the product of many years of advocacy by opponents of
Virginia’s 1902 arrangement. They needed the legislature to vote in two
consecutive years to place this type of measure on the ballot, and the
Democrat-controlled legislature [finally obliged in 2024 and
2025](https://boltsmag.org/virginia-constitutional-amendment-to-repeal-
lifetime-ban-on-voting/), motivated in large part by frustrations with
Youngkin’s rollback of voting rights.

“It only took 124 years,” Scott Surovell, Democratic majority leader in the
Virginia Senate, told _Bolts_ , "but we’ve finally eliminated Jim Crow from
the constitution of Virginia.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/RA18056-2400x1600.jpg)Virginia state Delegate Marcia
Price, left, reacts with Tram Nguyen, co-executive director of New Virginia
Majority, upon learning Amendment 3 had passed on Tuesday night. (Photo by
Shaban Athuman)

The amendment was endorsed by a broad coalition of groups, including the ACLU,
DSA, and NAACP, plus dozens of Democratic elected officials. It faced little
organized opposition, though the Republican Party of Virginia did encourage
voters to reject it,
[calling](https://x.com/VA_GOP/status/2104615548801929542) the reform
“deceptive, dangerous, and radical.”

Sheba Williams, a formerly disenfranchised nonprofit leader who helped lead
the campaign for the amendment, and who had pushed for years to advance it to
the ballot, added, “Many people say they want to work themselves out of a job,
and I’m honored to say I saw it come to fruition. Redemption is for everyone.”

By placing Amendment 3 on the ballot, Virginia lawmakers initiated the first
statewide vote on felony disenfranchisement in the U.S. since [California
voted in 2020](https://boltsmag.org/criminal-justice-reform-2020-election-
results/) to restore voting rights to people with felony convictions upon exit
from incarceration. Today, 24 states, now including Virginia, have that
policy. Another two states, Maine and Vermont, plus Puerto Rico and
Washington, D.C., never disenfranchise anyone over a felony conviction, even
while they’re incarcerated.

Prior to Tuesday, Virginia had been a significant national—[and
international](https://www.sentencingproject.org/reports/out-of-step-u-s-
policy-on-voting-rights-in-global-perspective/)—outlier for disenfranchising
so many people, for so long, over any of such a wide range of criminal
convictions.

“Virginia went from probably the worst in the nation as far as felony
disenfranchisement goes to being in line with a lot of its peers, with
disenfranchisement only being in place for the period of incarceration,” said
Tyler Richardett, the chief technology officer at Free Our Vote, a nonprofit
tech group that studies the scope of felony disenfranchisement and works to
help eligible voters access their rights.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/26014641829459-scaled.jpg)Speaker Don Scott, who
presided the Virginia House as it advanced the constitutional amendment to
restore voting rights, used to be disenfranchised himself for almost 20 years,
before then-Governor McDonnell restored his rights. (AP Photo/Steve Helber)

Tuesday’s landmark vote in Virginia builds on the federal ruling earlier this
year in partially fulfilling the intentions of Congress from the
Reconstruction era more than 150 years ago.

That Reconstruction Congress had, as a condition of readmitting southern
states into the Union, passed clear limits on felony disenfranchisement by
those states, because it correctly anticipated that they would do exactly what
Virginia went on to do—that is, suppress the voting power of formerly enslaved
people through harsh, targeted systems of disenfranchisement.

The judge’s ruling on this matter had already restored eligibility to many
thousands of Virginians earlier this year. Tuesday’s election codifies new and
more lenient rules in the state constitution, which could only be reversed via
another statewide vote.

Richardett and others say they expect that Amendment 3 will make it much
easier for affected people to understand their voting status. In Virginia and
beyond, _Bolts_ has found in reporting across the country on this issue,
people with past convictions often do not vote, [even if they
can](https://boltsmag.org/maine-prison-voting-rights/), because they either
assume they aren’t eligible or fear that they could be accused of voting
illegally—[or both](https://boltsmag.org/kentucky-voting-rights-restoration/).

“This ought to take a lot of guesswork out of the equation,” Richardett said.
“And for organizations doing the outreach, it ought to make the messaging much
easier.”

Martinez, who himself had exited prison with no clear sense of whether or how
he’d ever regain his voting rights, agreed.

“This is one less thing that's stressful on our plate when we get home,” he
said.

“When I came home,” Martinez added, “I wanted to be somebody who could
actually do something, who could have a voice. It finally feels like I do.”
